mainTopic: An אלמנה's below-value sales for her כתובה, and an agent who does less than he was told
overview: The amud opens by comparing two parts of a משנה about an אלמנה who sells her late husband's land to collect her כתובה. The גמרא concludes that both parts involve a lowered price. A sale stands when the loss comes out of her own share. It is void only when the loss comes out of the יתומים' property, and we do not cancel the earlier sales because of the last one. Then the גמרא returns to a question about agents. If an owner says 'sell a כּוֹר' and the agent sells only a half-כּוֹר, did the agent do him a favor, or can the owner object? רבי חנינא מסורא tries to answer from a משנה in מסכת מעילה: an agent sent with a gold דינר to buy a robe bought a robe for three and a cloak for three, and both are guilty of מעילה. The גמרא pushes the proof off by saying the robe was worth six and bought for three. It defends that reading against רבי יהודה's complaint of a 'small and bad' robe by explaining that 'bad' means bad in value. Finally it begins to show support from רבי יהודה's agreement in the case of legumes, and that discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The last clause seems to prove the first clause has no price cut
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא argues that since the סיפא is clearly about lowering the price, the רישא must be about a case where she did not lower the price.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the last clause is a case where she lowered the price, the first clause must be a case where she did not. The last clause teaches: her כתובה was 400 זוז. She sold to one person for a מנה, to another for a מנה, and to the last person something worth a מנה and a דינר for a מנה. The last sale is void, and all the others stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that the רישא is about the widow lowering the price. It points out that the סיפא already covers a lowered price.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סיפא clearly talks about lowering the price, since land worth 101 was sold for 100. If the רישא were also about lowering the price, the משנה would be repeating itself. So the רישא should be read as a case with no price cut.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of the משנה
The last clause of the משנה
She lowered the price (sold for less than it was worth)
A unit of money worth 100 זוז/דינרים
Her sale is void

steps.confusionAlert: Only the LAST sale is cancelled, not all of them. The earlier sales were at fair price.

phrases.english: But since the last clause is where she lowered the price,
the first clause must be where she did not lower it,
as the last clause teaches:
If her כתובה was four hundred זוז,
and she sold to this one for a מנה, and to that one for a מנה,
and to the last one, something worth a מנה and a דינר, for a מנה,
the sale of the last one is void,
and the sales of all the others stand!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the earlier reading (before this section) that the רישא is a case of a lowered price.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the רישא of the משנה is about the widow lowering the price
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The סיפא already covers a lowered price, so if the רישא did too, the משנה would be repeating itself.

steps.title: Both clauses involve a price cut; the difference is whose money was lost
steps.stepSummary: Both the רישא and סיפא are about lowering the price. The סיפא teaches that the sale is void only because she lowered the price with the יתומים' property.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Both the first and last clauses are cases where she lowered the price. The last clause teaches us this: the sale is void only because she lowered the price using the orphans' property. But if she lowers it using her own share, her sale stands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the challenge. Both clauses are about a lowered price, but each teaches a different point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the סיפא she had already been paid 300, so she was owed only 100 more. The extra דינר she gave away belonged to the יתומים, and that is why the last sale is void. In the רישא she gave away value from her own claim, so the sale stands.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches us (a new point)
The orphans (the husband's heirs)
With her own (her own share)
Her sale stands

phrases.english: No, both the first and last clauses are where she lowered the price,
and the last clause teaches us this:
The reason is that she lowered the price with the orphans' property,
phrases.notes: She was owed only 100 more, so the extra דינר of value was the orphans' money, not hers.

phrases.english: but with her own, her sale stands.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the סיפא a different lesson, so the two clauses are not repeating each other.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since both clauses are about a lowered price, the משנה seems to repeat itself.
steps.terutzMaskana: The סיפא teaches that the sale is void only when the price cut comes out of the יתומים' property.

steps.title: But the first clause already teaches that lesson
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the רישא already shows a sale stands when she lowers the price of her own share, so the סיפא adds nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: But you can already learn that from the first clause: if her כתובה was 200, and she sold land worth a מנה for 200, or land worth 200 for a מנה, she has received her כתובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer in step 2. The point it gave for the סיפא is already taught by the רישא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the רישא she sold land worth 200 for 100, and the sale stands. That already proves that a price cut out of her own share is valid. So why would the סיפא be needed to teach it?

keyTerms.meaning: You can learn it from there
She has received her כתובה (she can claim nothing more)

phrases.english: But you can already learn it from the first clause:
If her כתובה was two hundred,
and she sold land worth a מנה for two hundred,
or land worth two hundred for a מנה,
she has received her כתובה.

steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the סיפא teaches that a price cut from her own share is valid
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The רישא already shows exactly that, so the סיפא would be adding nothing.

steps.title: Without the last clause, we might have made a precautionary decree
steps.stepSummary: The סיפא is needed. Without it we might think the first sales should be cancelled too, as a decree to protect against problems with the last sale.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: there (in the first clause) the sale stands because she left this house completely. But here, we should decree on the first מנה because of the last מנה. So the משנה teaches us that we do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the סיפא is still needed. It blocks a mistaken idea we might have had.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the רישא her whole claim was settled in one sale, so there is no later sale to worry about. In the סיפא she sells in several stages. We might have cancelled even the early cheap sales so that people would not treat the last sale (which uses the יתומים' money) as valid too. The סיפא teaches that we make no such decree.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (a mistaken idea the משנה blocks)
She has removed herself / left completely
Let us make a decree (a protective rule)
Because of / for fear of

steps.whatToRemember: An אלמנה's below-value sale stands when the loss comes out of her own share, even across several sales. It is void only where the loss comes out of the יתומים' property, and we do not cancel the earlier sales because of the last one.

phrases.english: You might have said:
There, it is because she has removed herself
from this house completely,
phrases.notes: "This house" means her late husband's estate. With one sale, her whole claim is finished.

phrases.english: but here, let us decree
against the first מנה because of the last מנה,
phrases.notes: He means: cancel the first cheap sale, so that no one comes to treat the last one as valid too.

phrases.english: so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the סיפא is needed to rule out a possible decree.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: In a series of sales, we might cancel the earlier cheap sales because of the last one.
steps.terutzMaskana: No decree is made. The earlier sales stand and only the last one is void.

steps.title: Another version: selling more than asked is not the real question
steps.stepSummary: A second version of the question rules out the case where the agent sold more than asked. There he is clearly 'adding to his words,' and the part he was asked to sell is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: Don't ask about a case where the owner said 'Go sell a half-כּוֹר for me' and the agent sold a whole כּוֹר. He is clearly adding on to what he was told, so the first half stands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the question about an agent who did not follow his instructions exactly. It gives a second version, which first removes one case from the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling more than asked does not cancel what the owner wanted. The agent did the job and then added extra, so the half-כּוֹר the owner asked for is surely sold. This clears the way for the real question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: And there are those who say: a second version of the discussion
A לֶתֶךְ, half a כּוֹר (a measure of land or grain)
A כּוֹר, a large measure of land or grain
Adding to his words: the agent did what he was told plus more

phrases.english: And there are those who say:
Do not ask this question
in a case where he said to him:
"Go sell a half-kor for me"
phrases.notes: A לֶתֶךְ is half a כּוֹר, so the owner asked for the smaller amount.

phrases.english: and he sold a kor for him,
because he is certainly adding to his words.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: הָא לָא תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of the widow's sale (steps 1-4) and returns to the agent question raised on 98b, in a second version.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An agent who sells more than he was told is 'adding to his words,' and the sale of the amount the owner asked for is valid.

steps.title: The real question: the agent sold less than he was told
steps.stepSummary: The question is about an owner who said 'sell a כּוֹר' and an agent who sold only a half-כּוֹר. Did the agent do him a favor, or can the owner object to having more sale documents written against him?
steps.simpleTranslation: The real question is when the owner said 'Go sell a כּוֹר for me' and the agent sold only a half-כּוֹר. What is the law? Maybe the agent can say: 'I did you a favor. If it turns out you don't need the money, you could not have undone a sale.' Or maybe the owner can say: 'I don't want extra sale documents written against me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states the real question. It gives a reason for each side: the agent's sale might be valid, or the owner might be able to reject it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: selling less is good for the owner, because he keeps the rest of his land in case he finds he doesn't need the money. Side two: the owner wanted one sale. Now he may need a second sale and a second document, and he does not want many documents in his name.

keyTerms.meaning: I did what is good for you
Money (literally, זוזים coins)
Take it back, undo it
I am not comfortable with it, it doesn't suit me
Documents, here bills of sale

phrases.english: Where you should ask the question
is where he said to him: "Go sell a kor for me"
and he went and sold a half-kor for him. What is the law?
Do we say that he can say to him:
"I did what is good for you,
because if you turn out not to need the money,
you could not take it back"?
phrases.notes: He means: if I had sold everything, a completed sale could not be undone.

phrases.english: Or perhaps he can say to him:
"I am not comfortable
with documents multiplying against me."
phrases.notes: Now the owner may need another sale and another document, and he doesn't want many in his name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After ruling out selling more, this step asks about the opposite case, selling less.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is a sale valid when the agent sells less than he was told to sell?
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that an agent may stray from his instructions in a way that seems helpful, and still the owner may have a real reason to reject it.

steps.title: רבי חנינא מסורא brings the robe case from מסכת מעילה
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא מסורא cites a משנה: an agent given a gold דינר to buy a robe bought a robe for three and a cloak for three. Both the owner and the agent are guilty of מעילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא from סורא said: Come and hear. If someone gave his agent a gold דינר and said 'Bring me a robe,' and the agent brought a robe worth three and a cloak worth three, both of them are guilty of מעילה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא מסורא brings a משנה that may answer the question. The גמרא will work out the proof in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The gold דינר turned out to be הקדש money. The owner is guilty of מעילה too, so the agent's robe purchase counts as the owner's own act, even though the agent spent only half the money on it. That looks like an agent who does less than the full amount and still acts for the owner, like the half-כּוֹר case.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: a source is about to be brought
A gold דינר, worth six סלעים
A robe, an undergarment
A cloak
They committed מעילה, misusing הקדש property

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא מִסּוּרָא, תָּא שְׁמַע:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina of Sura said: Come and hear:
If one gave him a gold dinar
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in מסכת מעילה. The coin turns out to be הקדש money.

phrases.english: and said to him: "Bring me a robe,"
and he went and brought him
a robe for three and a cloak for three,
phrases.notes: Three סלעים each. The gold דינר was worth six, so the robe used only half the money.

phrases.english: both of them are guilty of me'ila.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא מִסּוּרָא, תָּא שְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the question from step 6 with a משנה.
steps.raayaObject: Whether an agent who does less than he was told (sells a half-כּוֹר instead of a כּוֹר) still acts for the owner.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in מסכת מעילה about an agent sent with a gold דינר to buy a robe.

steps.title: Why the owner's מעילה proves the agent is 'adding to his words'
steps.stepSummary: The owner is guilty of מעילה. That fits only if an agent who spends less than asked still did his job and simply added more. If he had gone against the owner's words, the owner would not be guilty.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense if an agent like this is doing his job and just adding to what he was told. That is why the owner is guilty of מעילה. But if he is going against what he was told, why is the owner guilty?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out how the משנה from Step 7 answers our question. The owner is guilty of מעילה, so the agent must have carried out his mission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An owner is guilty of מעילה through an agent only when the agent does what he was sent to do. In the משנה the agent spent only half the money on the robe, yet the owner is still guilty. This shows that doing less than the full amount counts as 'adding to his words,' so the owner of the half-כּוֹר sale would have no complaint.

keyTerms.meaning: He is carrying out his mission as an agent
Adding to the owner's words: he did what was asked, plus more
Going against the owner's words: he did not do what was asked
Is guilty of מעילה, wrongly using הקדש money for ordinary use
The owner, the one who sent the agent

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the key distinction of the whole סוגיא. An agent who adds to his words still keeps his mission, but one who goes against his words loses it.

phrases.english: Granted, if you say:
an agent in a case like this
is carrying out his mission,
and he is just adding to his words,
that is why the owner is guilty of מעילה.
But if you say:
he is going against his words,
why is he (the owner) guilty?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof that Step 7 began by citing the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: The question in Step 6: an agent told to sell a כּוֹר who sold only a half-כּוֹר.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in מעילה: the owner is guilty when the agent bought a robe for three and a cloak for three.

steps.title: The robe was worth six but bought for three
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed off. The agent found a robe worth the full six and paid only three, so the owner got exactly what he wanted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here we are dealing with a case where he brought him a robe worth six for the price of three.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof. It reads the משנה as a case where the agent got a bargain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the robe was really worth six, the owner received exactly the robe he asked for. So the משנה is not about an agent who did less than asked. It proves nothing about our half-כּוֹר case.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, what are we dealing with? This introduces a narrower reading of a source.
Worth six, bought for three: a bargain

phrases.english: Here, what are we dealing with?
Where he brought him
a robe worth six for three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects Step 8's proof by limiting the case of the משנה.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof only. The question from Step 6 stays open.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the agent gave the owner less than he asked for. If the robe was worth six, the owner got full value.

steps.title: Then why is the agent guilty?
steps.stepSummary: If the agent did exactly what he was told, why does the משנה say the agent is also guilty of מעילה?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why is the agent guilty?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new reading. The משנה says both the owner and the agent are guilty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The agent is guilty only for spending he did on his own, outside the mission. If the robe was a perfect fulfillment of the order, what did the agent do on his own?

keyTerms.meaning: If so: this introduces a challenge to the answer just given
The agent

phrases.english: If so, why is the agent guilty of מעילה?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case Step 9 set up.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading in Step 9 that the robe was worth six and bought for three.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the agent did exactly what was asked, nothing he did was on his own, so he should not be guilty. Yet the משנה says he is.

steps.title: The agent is guilty because of the cloak
steps.stepSummary: The agent is guilty for the cloak. He bought it on his own with the other three, and the owner never asked for it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers in one word: the agent's guilt comes from the cloak.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The robe was the owner's order, so the owner is guilty for it. The cloak was extra and was the agent's own idea, so the agent is guilty for those three coins.

keyTerms.meaning: The cloak, the extra item the agent bought

phrases.english: Because of the cloak.
phrases.notes: The טלית is the second item, the one the owner never asked for.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the guilt: each person is guilty for a different item.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the agent did his job, he should not be guilty at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner is guilty for the robe he ordered, and the agent is guilty for the cloak he bought on his own.

steps.title: רבי יהודה says the robe was small and bad
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the bargain reading from the סיפא. רבי יהודה says the owner can complain he got a 'small and bad' robe, so the robe was not worth six.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, look at the end of the משנה. רבי יהודה says: even here the owner is not guilty, because he can say, 'I wanted a big robe, and you brought me a small, bad one.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the סיפא of the same משנה to attack the reading in Step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה's argument works only if the three-coin robe was a lesser robe. If it were really worth six, the owner could not call it 'small and bad.' So the משנה seems to be about an agent who got less than asked, which brings back the original proof.

keyTerms.meaning: Look at the last part of the same משנה
A robe, the item the owner asked for
Small and bad, meaning worth less than he wanted

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two garments. The חלוק (robe) is what the owner ordered, and the טלית (cloak) is the extra item.

phrases.english: If so, say the last part:
Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: אַף בָּזֶה בַּעַל הַבַּיִת לֹא מָעַל,
phrases.english: Even in this case the owner is not guilty,
because he can say:
I was asking for a big robe,
and you brought me
a robe that is small and bad.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the bargain reading from Step 9 using the end of the same משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 9 that the robe was worth six and bought for three.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהודה's 'small and bad' complaint assumes the robe was worth less than six. That contradicts the bargain reading.

steps.title: 'Bad' means bad in value, not poor quality
steps.stepSummary: The word 'bad' in רבי יהודה's words means 'bad in value.' The owner can say: if this seller charged so little, my full six would have bought a robe worth twelve.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'bad' mean? Bad in value. The owner can say to the agent: 'If you had brought me a robe for six, it would surely have been worth twelve.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 12. It explains that 'bad' does not mean the robe was cheap junk. It means the owner lost out on value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The robe really was worth six, so the bargain reading from step 9 still stands. רבי יהודה's complaint is about a missed chance: a seller who sold a six-סלע robe for three would have sold a twelve-סלע robe for six. So by spending less, the agent changed the owner's instructions in a way that cost the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Bad in value. The robe is fine, but the owner got less than his money could have bought.
All the more so; surely.
Twelve (here, twelve סלעים).

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'bad' as 'poor quality.' The robe was really worth six. The owner's complaint is that six סלעים, spent at this cheap seller, would have bought a much better robe.

phrases.english: What is meant by 'bad'?
phrases.notes: This is the word 'bad' from רבי יהודה's 'small and bad' robe in step 12.

phrases.english: Bad in value,
for he can say to him:
If you had brought me one for six,

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן דַּהֲוָה שָׁוֵה תַּרְתֵּי סְרֵי.
phrases.english: all the more so it would have been worth twelve.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 12 by reading 'bad' as 'bad in value.'
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining a word: 'bad' means value lost, not low quality.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Small and bad' seemed to show the robe was really worth less than six, which would knock out the bargain reading.
steps.terutzMaskana: The robe was worth six. It is 'bad' only compared to the twelve-סלע robe the full six would have bought from this cheap seller. So the bargain reading stands.

steps.title: Support from רבי יהודה's agreement about legumes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the משנה's wording fits this reading. רבי יהודה agrees that with קטנית (legumes), both the owner and the agent are guilty of מעילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The wording is also exact, for the משנה teaches: רבי יהודה agrees that with legumes, both are guilty of מעילה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to bring support for its answer from the next line of the משנה. It quotes רבי יהודה's agreement about legumes, and the reasoning comes in the following lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה disagrees in the robe case but agrees in the legume case. So a robe has something that lets the owner complain, and legumes do not. This fits step 13: his complaint about the robe is that it is 'bad in value,' because the owner's full money would have bought a better robe from this cheap seller.

keyTerms.meaning: The wording is also exact; the source's wording supports this reading.
Agrees; admits in this case.
Legumes, like beans and lentils.
They are guilty of מעילה (misusing הקדש money).

phrases.english: It is also precise,
as it teaches:
Rabbi Yehuda agrees regarding legumes
that both of them are guilty of misusing consecrated property,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up the answer in step 13 with an exact reading of the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יהודה's 'bad' robe means 'bad in value' within the bargain case.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's line that רבי יהודה agrees both are guilty of מעילה in the case of legumes.
